CausalChain: Chronic liver injury and hypoxia -> Activation of HIF-1α -> Upregulation of ENTPD2 expression in tumor cells -> Conversion of extracellular ATP to 5’ AMP -> Recruitment and accumulation of MDSCs in the TME -> Suppression of CTL activity -> Reduced efficacy of ICIs
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that the combination of targeted pharmacological inhibition and CRISPR-mediated gene editing of ENTPD2, delivered via nanoparticle-based systems in hepatocellular carcinoma, will significantly lower MDSC recruitment and mitigate immunosuppressive conditions within the tumor microenvironment. This reduction in MDSC-mediated suppression is expected to restore CTL activity and consequently enhance the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors. The implementation of real-time bioimaging and multiplex biomarker monitoring will allow for precise modulation of therapy in response to dynamic changes within the tumor microenvironment, ensuring robust suppression of both primary and compensatory immunosuppressive pathways.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is characterized by chronic liver injury and hypoxia that activate HIF-1α, subsequently upregulating ENTPD2 expression and catalyzing the conversion of extracellular ATP to 5’ AMP. This cascade recruits immunosuppressive myeloid-derived suppressor cells (MDSCs) that hinder cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) activity and compromise the efficacy of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs). Here, we propose a novel, integrative therapeutic strategy that combines pharmacological inhibition and CRISPR-mediated knockdown of ENTPD2—delivered via targeted nanoparticle systems—with concurrent immune checkpoint blockade. Real-time multiplex biomarker monitoring and advanced imaging modalities will be employed to dynamically assess the tumor microenvironment (TME) and optimize treatment timing. This approach not only addresses the established ENTPD2-MDSC-CTL axis but also proactively monitors and mitigates compensatory immunosuppressive signals, thereby enhancing the overall therapeutic impact in HCC.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that pharmacological inhibition of ENTPD2 could reduce MDSC-mediated immunosuppression, thereby restoring CTL activity and enhancing ICI efficacy. The new hypothesis retains this fundamental causal chain—starting from chronic liver injury/hypoxia triggering HIF-1α and upregulating ENTPD2, which leads to extracellular ATP conversion, MDSC recruitment, and CTL suppression. However, the revised version enhances practicality and novelty by incorporating CRISPR-mediated gene editing to validate and reinforce ENTPD2 inhibition, nanoparticle-mediated delivery for targeted and efficient drug administration, and advanced real-time multiplex biomarker monitoring to dynamically assess and adjust the therapeutic response. This comprehensive approach not only addresses the original causal steps more robustly but also acknowledges and mitigates potential compensatory mechanisms within the TME.
